title: Your first 30 days in Korea: checklist
summary: Do these in order: book your residence card, get a phone, open a bank account, then sort out insurance, your address and transport.
steps: Week 1: book a visit on HiKorea for your {{외국인등록|alien registration}}. You must register within 90 days of arrival, and slots fill up — book early.
Week 1: get a prepaid SIM with your passport so you have a Korean number. Switch to a monthly plan once you have your card.
Week 2: sign or confirm your housing contract — you need an address on paper for registration.
After registration: open a {{통장|bank account}} with your residence card and passport.
Check your {{건강보험|health insurance}} status: students are covered from arrival, most other visas after 6 months.
Buy a T-money {{교통카드|transit card}} at any convenience store and save the emergency numbers (112, 119, 1345).

phrases.en: I'm here to register as a foreign resident.
Do you have a prepaid SIM?
I'd like to open a bank account.

checklist: Book your ARC visit on HiKorea
Lease or dorm letter (proof of address)
tips: Book the ARC first — every other step (phone plan, bank, delivery apps) gets easier once you have the card.
Many newcomers say the hardest part is phone identity checks; get a phone line in your own name as soon as you can.

title: How to get your residence card (ARC)
summary: Apply within 90 days of arrival. Book a visit on HiKorea, bring your passport, one photo, the fee and proof of address. The card takes about 3–4 weeks.
steps: Go to HiKorea → Visit Reservation and choose {{외국인등록|alien registration}} at the immigration office for your area.
Fill in the {{통합신청서|integrated application form}} (available at the office or on HiKorea).
Bring one passport-style {{사진|photo}} (3.5 × 4.5 cm, taken in the last 6 months) and your passport.
Bring proof of address, usually your {{임대차계약서|lease contract}} or a dorm certificate. Students also bring a {{재학증명서|certificate of enrollment}}.
Pay the {{수수료|fee}} — usually 30,000 won — at the office kiosk.
Your card arrives in about 3–4 weeks. Keep the receipt; it shows your registration is in progress.

phrases.en: When can I get my residence card?

checklist: 1 photo, 3.5 × 4.5 cm, taken in the last 6 months
Proof of address — lease or dorm letter
tips: Slots fill up fast — some people wait weeks. Check HiKorea several times a day; cancellations open up.
New arrivals can book as a non-member with their passport number.
Many reviews describe the staff as brusque and strict. Bring every document plus copies — one missing paper usually means booking again.
Walk-ins are usually turned away or wait for hours. Arrive 10 minutes early; numbers are sometimes called ahead of time.
Some offices sell a revenue stamp at a separate booth that may not take cards — carry some cash.
extra.tipsNote: Summarised from university guides, forums and map reviews. Experiences vary by office and day.
extra.warn: Registering after 90 days can bring a fine and cause trouble with later visa applications.

title: Extending your stay (visa extension)
summary: Apply before your permitted stay ends — online on HiKorea or at your immigration office. Late applications mean fines.
steps: Check the {{체류기간|period of stay}} on the back of your residence card or on HiKorea.
Apply for an {{연장|extension}} before it ends. Most people can apply from about 4 months before the expiry date.
Many visas can apply online: HiKorea → e-Application → {{체류기간 연장|extension of stay}}.
Prepare documents for your visa type (students: certificate of enrollment and transcript; workers: employment contract). Unpaid health insurance can delay approval.
Pay the fee online or at the office (often around 60,000 won — check HiKorea for your visa).
After approval, your new date is recorded; your card may get a sticker or a new date online.

phrases.en: I'm here to extend my stay.
When will I get the result?

checklist: Documents for your visa type (enrollment + transcript, or employment contract)
tips: Apply early — the HiKorea e-application often takes a few weeks to process.
Unpaid health insurance (₩500,000 or more) is reported to immigration and can limit your extension.
If HiKorea rejects an online upload, call 1345 before booking a visit.
extra.warn: Staying past the end of your permitted stay — even by a day — is illegal stay: fines and possible trouble re-entering Korea.

title: Wolse vs jeonse: how renting works
summary: Most foreigners rent with wolse: a deposit plus monthly rent. Jeonse is one large deposit and no rent — bigger money, bigger risk.
steps: {{월세|monthly rent}}: you pay a {{보증금|deposit}} (often 5–10 million won for a one-room) plus rent every month. The deposit comes back when you leave.
{{전세|jeonse}}: you pay a very large deposit (often over half the home's value) and no monthly rent. If the owner can't pay it back, you can lose it.
Small studios are called {{원룸|one-room}}; officetels are {{오피스텔|officetel}}. Short stays: {{고시원|goshiwon}} (tiny room, no deposit) or share houses.
Ask what the {{관리비|maintenance fee}} covers — water, internet and cleaning are sometimes included, gas and electricity usually not.
Real estate agents ({{부동산|real estate agency}}) charge a {{중개수수료|agent fee}} set by law as a percentage; ask for the amount before you sign.
Before signing, read the lease checklist guide.

phrases.en: What does the maintenance fee include?
I'm looking for a one-room with monthly rent.

tips: Apps such as Zigbang and Dabang list rooms, but many listings are bait — ask the agent to confirm the exact room before you visit.
Ask what the maintenance fee includes; "internet included" is common, gas and electricity usually are not.
Jeonse fraud has been in the news — be extra careful with large deposits and always check the property record.

title: Before you sign a lease: 5 checks
summary: Check who owns the home and whether it has debts, then register your address and get a fixed date so your deposit is protected.
steps: Ask for the {{등기부등본|property registration record}} (or look it up on iros.go.kr). The owner on it must match the person signing.
On the same record, look for a {{근저당|mortgage}}. A big loan plus your deposit can be more than the home is worth — that is the danger sign.
Read every line of the {{계약서|contract}}: deposit, rent, dates, who fixes what. Write special terms in the {{특약|special terms}} section.
After moving in, report your new address (for foreigners: {{체류지 변경신고|change of address report}}) within 15 days.
Get a {{확정일자|fixed date stamp}} on your contract at the community center or online. With the address report, it puts you in line to get your deposit back.

phrases.en: Can I see the property registration record?
Please put it in the special terms.
I'm here to get a fixed date stamp.

facts: fixed date stamp at the centre
checklist: Owner on the property record = person signing
Deposit, rent, dates and repairs written in the contract
Fixed date stamp on the contract
extra.warn: Without the address report and fixed date stamp, you may not get your deposit back first if the owner has debts.

title: Part-time work on a student visa
summary: You need permission before your first shift. Weekly hours depend on your program and Korean level, and some jobs are not allowed.
steps: Get {{시간제취업허가|part-time work permission}} before you start. Apply with your school's international office, then on HiKorea or at immigration.

Weekly limits depend on your degree program and TOPIK level: for example, undergraduates who meet the Korean requirement can work more weekday hours than those who don't. Your international office has the current table.
Language-program (D-4) students can usually apply only after about 6 months in Korea.
Some work is not allowed, such as construction, manufacturing, delivery, entertainment venues and private tutoring.
Sign a written {{근로계약서|employment contract}} — the permission application needs it.
Working without permission can cost you your visa, and your employer can be fined.

phrases.en: I want a part-time job — do I need permission?
Could you write an employment contract?

phrases.ko: 일주일에 몇 시간 일할 수 있어요?
phrases.en: How many hours a week can I work?

checklist: Permission form from your school's international office
TOPIK certificate if you have one
tips: Employers who say "permission isn't needed" are wrong — both you and the employer can be penalised.
Delivery and factory jobs pay well but are not allowed on a student visa.
extra.warn: Working without permission can cancel your visa.

title: Minimum wage, contracts and getting paid
summary: The 2026 minimum wage is 10,320 won an hour, for foreign workers too. Get a written contract and a payslip.
steps: The {{최저임금|minimum wage}} in 2026 is 10,320 won per hour. It applies to part-time and foreign workers.
If you work 15 hours or more a week, you also earn {{주휴수당|weekly holiday pay}} — roughly one extra paid day a week.
Your employer must give you a written {{근로계약서|employment contract}} with your pay, hours and duties.
You should get a {{임금명세서|payslip}} every payday showing how your pay was calculated.
Unpaid wages? Call the Ministry of Employment and Labor at 1350 (foreign languages available).

phrases.en: My pay hasn't come in yet.

title: National health insurance for foreigners
summary: Registered foreigners are enrolled automatically — students from arrival, most others after 6 months. Pay the monthly bill: unpaid premiums can affect your visa.
steps: With a residence card, you are enrolled in {{국민건강보험|National Health Insurance}} automatically: students from arrival, most other visa types after 6 months in Korea.
If you work for a company, you join through your job ({{직장가입자|workplace member}}) and the premium is taken from your pay.
Otherwise you are a {{지역가입자|regional member}} and get a monthly bill. Students pay a reduced rate.
Pay by bank transfer or automatic debit. Unpaid {{보험료|premiums}} can count against you when you extend your visa.
With insurance you pay only part of the bill at clinics, hospitals and pharmacies.
Questions in English: call 1577-1000 and choose the foreign-language option.

phrases.en: I'd like to pay the premium by automatic debit.

tips: Students pay a reduced premium — in 2026 universities quote about ₩79,000 a month; check your own bill.
Set up automatic debit so you never miss the 25th.
extra.warn: Unpaid premiums of ₩500,000 or more are reported to immigration and can limit a visa extension.

title: Seeing a doctor and buying medicine
summary: For common illness, go to a local clinic, then a pharmacy with the prescription. Big hospitals are for referrals and emergencies.
steps: Small clinics ({{의원|clinic}}) by specialty are the first stop: internal medicine ({{내과|internal medicine}}), ENT, dermatology. No appointment needed at most.
At reception show your residence card — insurance is applied automatically.
The doctor gives you a {{처방전|prescription}}; take it to any {{약국|pharmacy}} nearby.
Big university hospitals usually need a {{진료의뢰서|referral letter}} from a clinic for insurance rates.
At night or in an emergency, go to the {{응급실|emergency room}} or call 119.

phrases.en: I have a fever and a sore throat.
Is there a doctor who speaks English?

phrases.ko: 이 약은 하루에 몇 번 먹어요?
phrases.en: How many times a day do I take this medicine?

title: Opening a bank account and getting a phone plan
summary: Both are easiest with your residence card. Before it arrives, use a prepaid SIM; new accounts may start with a daily transfer limit.
steps: Bring your residence card, passport and a Korean phone number to the bank. Students often bring a certificate of enrollment; workers a contract.
New accounts for foreigners often start as a {{한도제한계좌|limited account}} with a low daily transfer limit; it can be raised later with proof of work or study.
Ask for a {{체크카드|debit card}} and set up mobile banking at the branch.
Phones: a {{선불|prepaid}} SIM needs only your passport. A {{후불|postpaid}} monthly plan usually needs your residence card.
Budget carriers ({{알뜰폰|budget phone plan}}) use the big networks and cost much less.

phrases.en: I'm here to open an account.
Can I get a debit card too?
Do you have an unlimited data plan?

tips: Banks near universities and in areas with many foreign residents are usually more used to foreign customers.
Ask for the daily transfer limit to be raised once you have a payslip or certificate of enrollment.

title: Emergency and help numbers
summary: 112 police, 119 fire and ambulance. 1345 for immigration questions, 1330 for 24-hour interpretation.
steps: {{경찰|police}}: 112. Text messages also work.
Fire and {{구급차|ambulance}}: 119. Interpretation is available — say your language.
Immigration questions in many languages: 1345 ({{출입국|immigration}} contact center).
Travel helpline and interpretation, 24 hours: 1330.
Unpaid wages and work problems: 1350. Health insurance: 1577-1000.
Save your address in Korean on your phone — it is the first thing a dispatcher asks for ({{주소|address}}).

title: Trash and recycling
summary: General trash goes in paid city bags, food waste goes separately, and recycling is sorted by type. Big items need a sticker.
steps: General trash goes in {{종량제 봉투|official trash bags}}, sold at convenience stores and marts. Buy the bags for your district.
{{음식물 쓰레기|food waste}} is separate — special bags, bins or a card-operated machine, depending on your building.
{{분리수거|recycling}}: plastic, cans, glass, paper and vinyl in separate bins. Rinse containers and remove labels.
Furniture and appliances are {{대형폐기물|large waste}}: report online or at the community center and attach the sticker.
Check your building's collection days and place — your landlord or neighbors will know.

phrases.en: Where do I throw away food waste?

tips: In Seoul houses and villas, clear PET bottles and vinyl go out only on set days — wrong-day trash is left behind.
Neighbours do notice: a bag with the wrong items may be returned or reported.
items: Rinse, remove the label, squash, close the cap — clear-PET bin
Rinse → plastic. Badly stained → general trash
General trash or the ice-pack box at the community centre
Empty the water, the bag goes to vinyl
Special non-burnable sack (sold at the community centre)

title: Getting around: transit cards
summary: Buy a T-money card at a convenience store, top it up with cash, and tap on and off for discounted transfers.
steps: Buy a {{교통카드|transit card}} (T-money) at a convenience store or subway station.
Top it up ({{충전|recharge}}) with cash at the store counter or a station machine.
Tap when you get on and when you get off the bus — tapping off gives you the {{환승|transfer}} discount on your next ride.
Many Korean debit cards can work as transit cards too.
Seoul also sells a monthly unlimited pass; check prices at a station.

phrases.en: Please top up my transit card.
Does this bus go to Gangnam Station?

title: Studying in Korea: language school or degree
summary: Start at a university language institute (D-4 visa) or apply for a degree (D-2). Degree programs usually ask for a TOPIK level.
steps: University {{어학당|language institute}} programs run in terms of about 10 weeks and start several times a year (D-4 visa).
Degree students ({{학부|undergraduate}} or {{대학원|graduate school}}) need a D-2 visa and an admission letter.
Most degree programs taught in Korean ask for a {{토픽|TOPIK}} level — often level 3 or higher for undergraduates. Check each school.
Scholarships: the Global Korea Scholarship (GKS) and many school {{장학금|scholarships}}.
Your school's international office helps with visas, part-time work permission and insurance.

phrases.en: I'd like to enroll in the language institute.
Which TOPIK level do I need?

title: Visiting the immigration office: what to expect
summary: Book on HiKorea, go to the office for your address, bring every document plus copies, and expect queues. Call 1345 first if you are unsure.
steps: Find your office: it depends on your {{체류지|registered address}}. HiKorea shows the right office when you make a {{방문 예약|visit reservation}}.
Book the exact task (registration, extension, change of status). A booking for one task cannot be used for another.
Prepare the {{통합신청서|integrated application form}} at home and print copies of every document.
Arrive 10–15 minutes early, take a number at the kiosk and wait for your counter.
Pay the {{수수료|fee}} at the kiosk or machine; keep the receipt until your new card arrives.

phrases.en: Which other documents do I need?

tips: Many reviews describe the counters as rushed and strict. Polite, short answers and a complete folder work best.
If you do not understand, ask them to write it down — or call 1345, which has interpreters.
Mornings at the start of the semester (March, September) are the busiest.
extra.tipsNote: Summarised from forums, university guides and map reviews.

title: Moving house: report your new address in 15 days
summary: Registered foreigners must report a new address within 15 days — online on HiKorea or at the community centre of the new address. It is free.
steps: After moving, report the {{체류지 변경신고|change of address}} within 15 days.
Online: HiKorea → e-Application → change of address, upload your new lease.
In person: go to the {{주민센터|community service centre}} of your new address with your residence card and lease.
Your card gets the new address on the back (or a sticker).
Also update your address with your bank, phone carrier and school or employer.

phrases.en: I'm here to report my new address.

extra.warn: Reporting late can bring a fine. The address report is also part of protecting your deposit.

title: Lost your residence card? Reissue it in 14 days
summary: Apply for a new card within 14 days of losing it. Book a visit on HiKorea and bring your passport, a photo and the fee.
steps: Book an immigration visit for {{재발급|reissue}} on HiKorea.
Bring your passport, the application form, one photo and proof of address.
Pay the {{수수료|fee}} — offices and university guides quote ₩30,000–35,000; check when you book.
Until the new card arrives, carry your passport as ID.
If the card was stolen, report it to the police (112) as well.

extra.warn: Applying late is a breach of the immigration rules and can bring a fine.

title: Utility bills: electricity, gas, water and maintenance
summary: In flats most bills come in one maintenance-fee bill; in houses and studios you may pay electricity and gas yourself. Set up automatic debit.
steps: Ask the landlord which bills are inside the {{관리비|maintenance fee}} and which are in your name.
{{전기 요금|electricity bill}}: KEPCO (call 123). Change the account holder when you move in.
{{가스|gas}}: call the city gas company for your area to connect and for the safety check; someone must be home.
{{수도 요금|water bill}}: often included in the maintenance fee, or billed every two months.
Pay by {{자동이체|automatic debit}}, bank transfer to the bill's account, or bill-pay in banking apps.
Take photos of the meters on move-in and move-out day.

phrases.en: What does the maintenance fee include?
I'm calling to connect the gas.

tips: Winter gas bills surprise many newcomers — floor heating (ondol) left on all day is expensive.
Bills often arrive as KakaoTalk or text messages rather than paper.

title: Paying your health insurance premium
summary: Foreign members on a regional plan pay in advance: each month's premium is due by the 25th of the month before. Automatic debit is the easiest way and gives a small discount.
steps: The {{고지서|bill}} comes by post, email or app. Regional members who are foreigners pay each month by the 25th of the month before; after that a {{연체금|late fee}} is added daily.
Ways to pay: {{자동이체|automatic debit}}, the {{가상계좌|virtual account}} on the bill, bank or ATM, or a card (a 0.5–0.8% card fee is added).
Set up automatic debit through NHIS (1577-1000, website or a branch) — it gives a small monthly discount.
Students: universities publish the yearly student premium (about ₩79,000 a month in 2026); check your own amount.
Leaving Korea for good? Report it so you are not billed afterwards.

phrases.en: I want to pay by automatic debit.
I'd like to get the bill by email.

tips: Several students report bills arriving late at a new address — set up email bills to avoid surprises.
extra.warn: Unpaid premiums of ₩500,000 or more are reported to immigration; extensions can then be limited (often to 6 months or less).

title: When phone identity checks (PASS) fail
summary: Korean apps verify you with a phone line in your own name. Most failures come from a prepaid or foreign number, or a name typed differently from your card.
steps: Most sites use {{본인인증|identity verification}} through your phone carrier or the PASS app.
It only works with a {{휴대폰|mobile phone}} line registered in your own name with your residence card number.
Type your name exactly as on your residence card — spaces and order matter.
If it loops forever, switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data, update or reinstall PASS, then retry.
Some services simply do not accept foreigners online — call their customer centre and ask for another way.

tips: Budget carriers (알뜰폰) are cheaper and usually work for verification, but some shops limit which nationalities they sign up — ask first.
A line in a friend's name will not pass checks in your name.

title: Ordering food delivery
summary: Baemin and Coupang Eats are the main apps. You need a Korean phone number for sign-up; type your address in Korean and add the building door code.
steps: Install {{배달의민족|Baemin}} or {{쿠팡이츠|Coupang Eats}} and verify your phone number.
Enter your address in Korean, then the {{동|building}} and {{호|unit}} number.
Add the {{공동현관 비밀번호|building door code}} in the request note so the rider can get in.
Check the {{최소주문금액|minimum order}} and the {{배달팁|delivery fee}}.
Write a note such as "문 앞에 두고 벨 눌러 주세요" (leave it at the door and ring).

phrases.ko: 문 앞에 두고 벨 눌러 주세요.
phrases.en: Leave it at the door and ring the bell.

tips: Ordering together with a friend is common to reach the minimum order.

title: Eating out in Korea: how restaurants work
summary: Water and side dishes are free, you call staff with a bell, pay at the counter after eating, and never tip.
steps: Water is free — often {{셀프|self-service}} from a corner or fridge.
Press the {{호출벨|call bell}} on the table to order or ask for something.
Basic {{반찬|side dishes}} (kimchi, lettuce) are refilled free; costly ones (egg stew, meat) may cost extra.
Many BBQ places need at least two portions ({{인분|servings}}).
Pay at the {{계산대|counter}} on your way out. No tipping — leaving cash may make staff chase you.

title: Korean BBQ: how to order and eat
summary: Order meat by the portion, grill it at the table, wrap it in lettuce, and finish with a stew, cold noodles or fried rice.
steps: Popular cuts: {{삼겹살|pork belly}}, {{목살|pork neck}}, {{갈비|marinated ribs}}. Order at least two portions.
Staff may grill for you; otherwise use the tongs and cut with {{가위|scissors}}.
Make a {{쌈|lettuce wrap}}: lettuce, meat, a little ssamjang, garlic — one bite.
Finish the meal with {{된장찌개|soybean stew}}, {{냉면|cold noodles}} or fried rice.

phrases.en: Two portions of pork belly, please.
Could you change the grill plate?

title: Convenience-store food like a local
summary: Triangle kimbap, lunch boxes and cup noodles with free hot water — watch for 1+1 and 2+1 deals.
steps: Open {{삼각김밥|triangle kimbap}} by pulling tab 1, then the two sides.
{{도시락|lunch boxes}} can be heated in the store microwave.
Cup noodles: hot water and chopsticks are free at the counter area.
Look for {{1+1|buy one get one}} and {{2+1|buy two get one}} stickers.
Some stores near the Han River have instant-ramen cookers.

title: Gwangjang Market: what to eat (and how not to overpay)
summary: Seoul's best-known food market: mung-bean pancakes, mini kimbap and beef tartare. It has had price controversies — check prices before you order.
steps: Get off at {{종로5가역|Jongno 5-ga Station}} (Line 1) or Euljiro 4-ga.
Classics: {{빈대떡|mung-bean pancake}}, {{마약김밥|mini kimbap}}, {{육회|beef tartare}} alley, {{칼국수|knife-cut noodles}}.
Look at the menu board for the price and, for platters, the weight (Seoul asked stalls to show it).
Order one dish per stall and move on — sharing small plates is the fun.
Bring cash; some stalls still don't take cards.

tips: Since 2023 the market has repeatedly been in the news for small portions and pushy selling (e.g. a ₩15,000 mixed-pancake platter). Seoul introduced weight labels, mystery shoppers and stall-name boards.
Locals often suggest Mangwon or Gyeongdong market for a calmer, cheaper market meal.
Ask the price before you sit down, and don't feel obliged to order extra.
extra.tipsNote: From news reports (2023–2025) and online reviews.

title: Euljiro: old-school eateries and Pyongyang cold noodles
summary: Printing-shop alleys with decades-old restaurants: grilled pollack and beer outdoors, and one of Seoul's oldest Pyongyang naengmyeon places.
steps: Get off at {{을지로3가역|Euljiro 3-ga Station}} (Lines 2 and 3).
{{노가리 골목|dried-pollack alley}}: plastic tables on the street, grilled pollack with beer — best on summer evenings.
Try {{평양냉면|Pyongyang cold noodles}}: a mild beef broth. Woo Lae Oak (since 1946) is a famous one nearby.
Many small bars hide upstairs in old printing buildings — look for signs on the stairs.

tips: Pyongyang naengmyeon tastes plain at first — many people say it grows on you by the second bowl.

title: Mangwon Market and the Han River
summary: A neighbourhood market with cheap snacks, close to Mangwon Han River Park — a relaxed local alternative to the tourist markets.
steps: Get off at {{망원역|Mangwon Station}} (Line 6), exit 2.
Snack on {{호떡|sweet pancakes}}, fried chicken pieces, croquettes and tteokbokki.
Buy fruit or side dishes for a picnic, then walk 15 minutes to {{한강공원|Han River Park}}.
Explore the cafés on the street locals call Mangridan-gil.

tips: Reviews say it is less crowded with tourists, so you can browse at your own pace.

title: Busan food: pork soup, wheat noodles and the fish market
summary: Busan's classics are dwaeji gukbap (pork rice soup), milmyeon (cold wheat noodles), fish cakes and raw fish at Jagalchi.
steps: {{돼지국밥|pork rice soup}}: add the chives (locals call them 정구지), salted shrimp and a little chilli paste.
{{밀면|wheat cold noodles}}: Busan's version of naengmyeon, born after the Korean War.
{{어묵|fish cakes}}: try them hot from street stalls or bakeries that specialise in them.
{{자갈치시장|Jagalchi Market}}: pick fish downstairs, eat it upstairs (a table fee applies).
{{씨앗호떡|seed-filled pancake}}: a Nampo-dong street snack.

tips: At fish markets, agree the price and weight before they cut the fish.

title: Day trip: Suwon Hwaseong Fortress
summary: A UNESCO World Heritage fortress about an hour from Seoul. Walk the 5.7 km wall, visit the palace and end on Suwon's fried-chicken street.
steps: Take Line 1 to {{수원역|Suwon Station}}, then a bus or taxi to the palace area (or Line 1 to Hwaseo Station for the west gate).
Start at {{화성행궁|Hwaseong Haenggung Palace}} (09:00–18:00, open every day).
Walk part of the wall: the city suggests 60-minute and 120-minute routes; the full loop is about 5.7 km.
On weekends the palace often opens at night in season — check the city site.
Eat at {{통닭거리|chicken street}} near the palace.

phrases.en: How do I get to Hwaseong Haenggung?

tips: Comfortable shoes — the wall has steep parts.
Visit in autumn for the Suwon Hwaseong Cultural Festival, but expect crowds.

title: Day trip: Gapyeong and Chuncheon by train
summary: The ITX-Cheongchun train takes you to Gapyeong (Nami Island) and Chuncheon (dakgalbi). Book weekend seats early.
steps: Take the {{ITX-청춘|ITX-Cheongchun}} from Yongsan or Cheongnyangni, or the slower Gyeongchun Line subway.
Gapyeong Station → bus or taxi to the ferry for {{남이섬|Nami Island}}.
The Garden of Morning Calm: from Cheongpyeong Station by bus or taxi (about 25 min).
In Chuncheon, eat {{닭갈비|spicy stir-fried chicken}} and {{막국수|buckwheat noodles}}.

phrases.ko: 청춘 열차 표 두 장 주세요.

title: Day trip: Dumulmeori, where two rivers meet
summary: Morning mist on the river, an old zelkova tree and lotus gardens — 15 minutes' walk from Yangsu Station.
steps: Take the Gyeongui–Jungang Line to {{양수역|Yangsu Station}} and walk about 15 minutes.
Go early for {{물안개|river mist}} at sunrise.
Visit {{세미원|Semiwon}} lotus gardens next door (summer is best).
Rent a bike — the riverside path runs along the old railway.

title: Day trip: Ganghwa Island
summary: Dolmens (UNESCO), an old temple and a local market — about 1.5 hours by bus from Sinchon.
steps: Take an intercity bus from the {{신촌|Sinchon}} area to Ganghwa (about 1.5 hours).
See the {{고인돌|dolmens}}, part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Visit {{전등사|Jeondeungsa Temple}}, one of Korea's oldest temples.
Try purple-radish kimchi at {{풍물시장|the traditional market}}.

phrases.en: Where do I catch the bus to Ganghwa?

title: Busan: Yeongdo and Huinnyeoul Culture Village
summary: A free cliffside village above the sea, a coastal walk and Taejongdae cliffs — a short bus ride from Nampo.
steps: Take a bus from {{남포동|Nampo-dong}} across the bridge to Yeongdo.
Walk through {{흰여울문화마을|Huinnyeoul Culture Village}} — free to enter, people live here.
Follow the coastal walking path below the village.
Continue to {{태종대|Taejongdae}} for cliffs and a lighthouse.

tips: Residents ask visitors to keep voices down and not photograph inside homes.

title: Han River picnic like a local
summary: Spread a mat, order fried chicken to the park's delivery zone, cook ramen at the riverside convenience store and take your trash home.
steps: Pick a park: Yeouido, Banpo (rainbow fountain in season) or Ttukseom.
Order {{치킨|fried chicken}} to the park's {{배달존|delivery zone}} and meet the rider there.
Use the ramen cooker at a riverside {{편의점|convenience store}}.
Rent a {{따릉이|Seoul public bike}} with the app.
Separate your trash at the park bins or take it home.

phrases.en: Please bring it to the delivery zone.
